name: AWS - SQS
scope: A person with INTERMEDIATE proficiency level in AWS SQS as a competency should be able to explain SQS’s role in distributed systems, differentiate Standard vs FIFO queues and configure core settings like retention, visibility timeout, delivery delay, DLQs, and queue policies (including IAM and KMS encryption). They should manage message lifecycle (send, receive, delete, visibility timeout, DLQ), use long polling, batch APIs, and handle deduplication and ordering (message group IDs, deduplication IDs), as well as design idempotent producers and consumers with appropriate error handling, retries, and backoff strategies. They should integrate SQS with AWS services (SNS, Lambda, Step Functions), use IaC tools (CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform) for queue provisioning, and manage environments and naming/tagging for governance. They should monitor with CloudWatch metrics, alarms, and logs, troubleshoot common issues (backlogs, DLQ spikes, misconfigurations), and optimize for cost, throughput, and latency. They should perform integration and contract testing (using mocks, local simulators), manage operational tasks (purging, scaling, DLQ reprocessing), and participate in incident response and DR planning. They should document queue purposes, schemas, and SLAs, collaborate with other teams on contracts and error handling, and contribute to runbooks and knowledge sharing. They should understand SQS limits, anti-patterns, and basic local development practices, and use SDKs in at least one language with robust error handling and configuration.

{"sections":[{"name":"Core SQS Fundamentals & Mental Models","scope_included":"- Understand SQS’s role in distributed systems
  - Articulate SQS as a fully managed, highly available, region-scoped message queuing service
  - Explain how SQS decouples producers and consumers to improve resilience, scalability, and fault isolation
  - Differentiate clearly between synchronous request/response vs asynchronous, queue-based communication

- Grasp core SQS concepts and entities
  - Queue, message, attributes, message body, message ID, receipt handle
  - Producers, consumers, pollers, workers
  - Visibility timeout, retention period, delay, long polling
  - Dead-letter queues (DLQs) and redrive policy

- Delivery guarantees and behavior
  - Explain SQS delivery model: at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering for standard queues
  - Understand exactly-once processing as an application-level property (idempotency), not a transport guarantee for standard queues
  - Recognize trade-offs between throughput, ordering, and duplication

- When to use SQS vs other AWS messaging services
  - Distinguish SQS vs SNS (queue vs pub/sub)
  - Distinguish SQS vs EventBridge (event bus vs queue)
  - Distinguish SQS vs Kinesis (queues vs streams) at a conceptual level
  - Identify appropriate use cases for SQS in common architectures (decoupling microservices, buffering workloads, batch processing, throttling downstream systems)

- Consistency and durability expectations
  - Explain message durability guarantees and replication across multiple AZs
  - Understand eventual consistency considerations in visibility and metrics","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Queue Types & Configuration","scope_included":"- Standard vs FIFO queues
  - Describe characteristics of standard queues: high throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering
  - Describe characteristics of FIFO queues: strict ordering, limited throughput, exactly-once processing semantics within constraints
  - Understand trade-offs and select appropriate queue type based on business requirements (ordering, deduplication, throughput, latency, cost)

- Core queue-level configuration options
  - Configure message retention period for different workloads and compliance needs
  - Configure default visibility timeout at queue level based on processing time
  - Configure delivery delay at queue level to introduce scheduled work or simple deferrals
  - Configure maximum message size and recognize when to use external storage (such as S3) for large payloads

- FIFO-specific configuration
  - Use message group IDs to control parallelism while preserving ordering within groups
  - Use message deduplication IDs and deduplication interval effectively
  - Understand throughput constraints of FIFO queues with and without high-throughput FIFO

- Redrive and DLQ-related queue configuration
  - Configure DLQs and maxReceiveCount appropriately for different workloads
  - Understand implications of reprocessing messages from DLQs

- Access and connection configuration
  - Understand and configure queue policies for cross-service and cross-account access at an intermediate level
  - Use VPC endpoints (Gateway and Interface endpoint) conceptually for private SQS access in VPC (even if not deeply tuning networking)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Message Lifecycle, Delivery Semantics & Ordering","scope_included":"- End-to-end message lifecycle
  - Describe lifecycle: send → store durably → receive (poll) → invisible during processing → delete or become visible again → possible DLQ
  - Explain how visibility timeout controls reappearance of messages for reprocessing
  - Understand impact of partial failures (consumer crash, network issue) on visibility and redelivery

- Visibility timeout and processing time
  - Size default visibility timeout to typical processing duration with safety margin
  - Adjust visibility timeout dynamically from consumer side for long-running tasks
  - Explain implications of using too-short or too-long visibility timeouts (duplication vs slow retries)

- Long polling vs short polling
  - Configure ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds for long polling and articulate benefits (reduced cost, reduced empty responses, smoother load)
  - Decide when to use long polling at queue-level vs API-level
  - Understand interaction of long polling with consumer concurrency and scaling

- Message ordering
  - For standard queues, handle out-of-order messages in consumer logic when ordering is important
  - For FIFO queues, ensure correct usage of message group IDs to balance parallelism and ordering
  - Avoid design patterns that unintentionally break ordering guarantees (such as mixing group IDs improperly or using multiple queues without appropriate design)

- Message expiration and retention
  - Configure and reason about message retention period vs business SLAs
  - Understand how SQS discards messages after retention and how that interacts with DLQ configuration

- Deduplication semantics (FIFO)
  - Understand how content-based deduplication vs explicit deduplication IDs work within deduplication interval
  - Design message IDs and deduplication IDs to avoid unintended drops or duplicates at application level","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Producer Responsibilities & Design","scope_included":"- Producer-side API usage and patterns
  - Use SendMessage, SendMessageBatch and understand limits on batch size and payload
  - Set message attributes for metadata, routing hints, tracing, and context propagation
  - Design message bodies and schemas (JSON, Avro, or other structured formats) with forwards/backwards compatibility in mind

- Reliability and idempotency from producer perspective
  - Design producers to handle send failures, retries, and duplication without data loss
  - Use correlation IDs or business keys to support idempotent processing downstream
  - Ensure producers avoid reliance on synchronous acknowledgement of business completion from SQS

- Throughput and batching strategies
  - Aggregate multiple logical events into batched messages where appropriate and safe
  - Tune batch size to balance cost, latency, and downstream processing constraints

- Handling large payloads and external storage
  - Recognize need to store large bodies in an external store (such as S3) and send references/pointers through SQS
  - Consider atomicity and consistency between SQS messages and external stores

- Schema evolution and versioning considerations
  - Include schema versioning mechanisms or metadata to support evolution of message formats over time
  - Ensure compatibility between multiple producer versions and consumer versions during migrations

- Security from producer side
  - Use IAM roles/instance profiles/identity-based access for applications producing to SQS
  - Avoid embedding credentials in configuration or code
  - Understand basic implications of KMS-encrypted queues on producer configuration and permissions","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Consumer Responsibilities & Processing Patterns","scope_included":"- Consumer-side API usage and patterns
  - Implement long-polling ReceiveMessage with appropriate max number of messages and wait time
  - Use DeleteMessage and DeleteMessageBatch correctly with receipt handles
  - Use ChangeMessageVisibility when extending processing time is necessary

- Concurrency and scaling at consumer level
  - Design consumer workers with configurable concurrency (threads, processes, containers, or Lambda concurrency)
  - Understand impact of concurrency on visibility, ordering (especially for FIFO with group IDs), and downstream systems

- Idempotent and resilient processing
  - Implement idempotent consumers that can safely reprocess messages without causing inconsistent state or side effects
  - Use idempotency keys, deduplication tables, or state checks in downstream stores
  - Avoid processing side effects before ensuring all preconditions and validations are complete

- Backoff and retry strategies at consumer level
  - Implement exponential backoff for transient failures while honoring visibility timeouts
  - Distinguish between retriable and non-retriable errors and act accordingly (reject to DLQ vs retry)

- Batch processing and partial failures
  - Process batches of messages efficiently while handling partial failures within a batch
  - Apply strategies such as per-message error handling, splitting failed batches, or selectively re-queuing

- Consumer performance and resource management
  - Monitor processing time, memory, and downstream dependencies (databases, APIs)
  - Adjust concurrency and visibility to optimize throughput without overloading dependencies

- Event-driven compute integrations
  - Understand how Lambda event source mapping for SQS works conceptually (batch size, concurrency, failure behavior)
  - Design consumer logic compatible with Lambda and container-based workers","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Error Handling, DLQs & Retry Strategies","scope_included":"- Dead-letter queues (DLQs)
  - Configure DLQs and redrive policies to capture poisoned messages or persistent failures
  - Define maxReceiveCount values appropriate to business tolerance for retries and processing latency
  - Understand how messages transition to DLQs and how misconfiguration can silently drop or endlessly retry messages

- Error categorization and handling
  - Classify errors (transient, persistent, non-retriable, external dependency failures)
  - Implement differentiated handling paths for each error type

- Retry patterns and backoff strategies
  - Implement exponential backoff and jitter to reduce thundering-herd behavior and avoid hot loops
  - Combine visibility timeout tuning with backoff to avoid premature redelivery or excessively delayed processing

- DLQ processing and recovery
  - Define and implement processes for inspecting, triaging, and reprocessing DLQ messages
  - Ensure safe reprocessing from DLQs without causing repeated failures or data corruption
  - Use separate tools, scripts, or tasks to move messages between queues for recovery procedures

- Observability of failures
  - Configure metrics, alarms, and dashboards to track DLQ inflow, approximate age, and backlog
  - Use failure patterns from DLQs to improve upstream validations, schema checks, and consumer robustness","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Security, Access Control & Compliance","scope_included":"- IAM-based access control
  - Define least-privilege IAM policies for producers, consumers, and administrative tools
  - Use resource-based policies on SQS queues for service-to-service or cross-account access at a basic-to-intermediate depth
  - Understand how AWS principals (roles, users, services) are authorized to perform SQS actions (SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage, PurgeQueue, GetQueueAttributes, etc.)

- Encryption and data protection
  - Enable and reason about server-side encryption (SSE) with KMS on queues
  - Understand KMS key policies impact on SQS usage by applications
  - Recognize implications of encryption on latency and cost in typical workloads

- Network and connectivity considerations
  - Understand benefits of using VPC endpoints for SQS to avoid public internet paths from within VPCs
  - Understand how security groups and NACLs work in combination with VPC endpoints for SQS (conceptually, not necessarily deep networking tuning)

- Compliance and data governance
  - Align message retention and DLQ retention policies with data governance and compliance requirements
  - Avoid sending sensitive data where not necessary; design messages to minimize secrets and PII in transit and at rest

- Auditing and change control
  - Recognize CloudTrail logging for SQS management operations and use it in investigations
  - Incorporate SQS configuration changes into version-controlled IaC for auditable changes","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Integrations & Event-Driven Architectures with SQS","scope_included":"- Integration with AWS services
  - Use SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern for decoupled broadcasting to multiple queues
  - Use SQS as event source for Lambda functions and understand configuration parameters influencing concurrency and failure behavior
  - Integrate SQS into Step Functions workflows conceptually where queue-based buffering is required
  - Interact with S3, DynamoDB, RDS, and other services from SQS consumers in a reliable and idempotent manner

- Architecture patterns using SQS
  - Point-to-point messaging using SQS as the intermediary between microservices
  - Work queue pattern with worker fleets scaling horizontally
  - Queue-based throttling to protect downstream systems from overload
  - Compensating transaction patterns where SQS is used to orchestrate or serialize compensating work

- Hybrid and multi-queue patterns
  - Design solutions with multiple queues for priority handling, separate workflows, or isolation between tenants or modules
  - Use DLQs as separate queues with their own processing flows and SLAs

- Migration and coexistence
  - Integrate SQS into systems previously using other messaging technologies at a basic-to-intermediate level
  - Understand high-level strategies for bridging between on-prem or other cloud queues and SQS

- Event modeling and contract design
  - Model events and commands carried over SQS messages with clear boundaries
  - Establish message contracts and ownership between producing and consuming teams in an organization","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Performance, Scalability & Cost Optimization","scope_included":"- Throughput and scaling characteristics
  - Understand horizontal scalability of standard queues and per-shard/group constraints of FIFO queues
  - Estimate and reason about achievable throughput based on API limits, batch sizes, and consumer concurrency

- Latency considerations
  - Understand impact of long polling wait times and batch sizes on end-to-end latency
  - Balance cost vs latency by tuning poll frequency, wait times, and batch sizes

- Cost optimization
  - Identify primary cost drivers: number of API calls, payload size, KMS encryption, data transfer
  - Reduce costs by using long polling, batching, and avoiding unnecessary empty receives
  - Consider trade-offs between more queues vs fewer queues, and their operational and cost implications

- Backlog management
  - Monitor queue depth and age of oldest message to detect backlog buildup
  - Adjust consumer fleet size, concurrency, and batch sizes to keep within processing SLAs

- Avoiding anti-patterns
  - Avoid using SQS for storing large datasets or long-term storage instead of short-lived work items
  - Avoid designs that require transactional coordination between SQS and other stores without appropriate patterns

- Basic tuning for FIFO queues
  - Adjust message group strategies to maximize parallelism without breaking required ordering
  - Understand high-throughput FIFO considerations at a conceptual level","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Monitoring, Observability & Troubleshooting","scope_included":"- Core metrics and alarms
  - Use CloudWatch metrics for ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, NumberOfMessagesSent/Received/Deleted, and DLQ metrics
  - Define alarms on key thresholds (backlog size, message age, DLQ inflow) to detect issues proactively

- Logging and tracing
  - Implement application logs in consumers and producers that include message IDs, correlation IDs, and important attributes
  - Integrate distributed tracing where applicable to trace message flow across services

- Health checks and operational visibility
  - Define health indicators for consumers (processing rate, error rates, latency, concurrency utilization)
  - Use dashboards to visualize queue and consumer health together

- Troubleshooting techniques
  - Investigate stuck messages, growing backlogs, or DLQ spikes using metrics, logs, and queue inspection
  - Identify misconfigured visibility timeouts, redrive policies, or consumer bugs causing repeated retries
  - Recognize common configuration issues such as missing permissions, incorrect endpoints, or region mismatches

- Capacity and resiliency verification
  - Perform basic load tests and failure simulations to validate that SQS-based components behave correctly under stress and partial failures
  - Use findings from tests to iterate on visibility timeout, concurrency, and backoff settings","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Setup, Configuration & IaC Tooling","scope_included":"- Queue provisioning and configuration
  - Create and configure SQS queues through AWS Console with all core options at intermediate depth
  - Use CLI and SDKs to manage and inspect queues programmatically

- Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
  - Define SQS queues, DLQs, policies, and related configurations using at least one IaC tool (such as CloudFormation, AWS CDK, Terraform) at a practical level
  - Parameterize queue configuration (retention, visibility, encryption, DLQ) to support multiple environments (dev, test, prod)
  - Integrate SQS provisioning into CI/CD pipelines for consistent, repeatable deployments

- Environment management
  - Maintain separate queues per environment and avoid cross-environment interference
  - Ensure naming conventions and tagging practices enable discoverability, cost attribution, and governance

- SDKs and language bindings
  - Use SQS SDKs in at least one primary language in a robust way (error handling, pagination, batching)
  - Understand versioning and configuration (timeouts, connection pooling, retries) at SDK level for producers and consumers

- Local and sandbox setup (high-level)
  - Set up basic local or sandbox environments for development and testing that mimic SQS usage patterns conceptually (even if not at full fidelity)
  - Use tools or mocks to emulate SQS behavior where a real AWS account is not suitable (at least at pattern level)","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Local Development, Testing Strategies & Test Tooling","scope_included":"- Unit and integration testing
  - Design code for producers and consumers to be testable independently of real SQS
  - Use mocks, fakes, or local simulators for SQS APIs in unit tests
  - Perform integration tests against real SQS queues in isolated environments where appropriate

- Contract and compatibility testing
  - Establish and verify message schema contracts between producers and consumers
  - Test evolution of message formats to avoid breaking changes across services

- Failure and resilience testing
  - Simulate message retries, DLQ routing, and consumer restarts in test environments
  - Validate behavior under visibility timeout expirations, partial failures, and duplicated deliveries

- Performance and load testing (basic)
  - Conduct basic throughput and latency tests to verify that queue and consumers meet expected SLAs
  - Use testing results to adjust configuration and application code

- Developer experience and tooling
  - Use scripts or small utilities to send, receive, and inspect messages for debugging purposes
  - Maintain reusable helpers or libraries inside the team to avoid repeated boilerplate for SQS interactions","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Operations, Maintenance & Incident Management","scope_included":"- Routine operational tasks
  - Safely purge queues when required, understanding irreversible effects
  - Rotate or replace queues when large-scale configuration changes are needed, with minimal downtime and data loss

- Capacity management and scaling
  - Monitor and adjust consumer fleet sizes and concurrency based on observed load
  - Plan for spikes and seasonal patterns in message volume

- Incident management
  - Participate in incident response when SQS-based components degrade or fail
  - Use metrics, logs, and configuration inspection to identify root causes involving SQS
  - Implement short-term mitigations (temporary scaling, manual DLQ reprocessing, configuration tweaks) while planning long-term fixes

- Reliability and availability practices
  - Understand regional dependency of SQS and implications for DR strategies at a conceptual level
  - Participate in designing or operating multi-AZ and, when necessary, multi-region patterns that rely on SQS

- Lifecycle and housekeeping
  - Periodically review queues for unused or obsolete resources and retire them safely
  - Validate DLQs to ensure they are drained or addressed regularly and do not silently accumulate critical failures","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Collaboration, Documentation & Review Practices","scope_included":"- Documentation expectations
  - Document queue purposes, owners, retention policies, DLQ behavior, and SLAs for each queue
  - Capture message schema definitions and evolution history in shared repositories

- Cross-team communication
  - Collaborate with producer and consumer teams to define message contracts, error handling agreements, and DLQ ownership
  - Communicate SQS-related constraints (ordering, throughput, at-least-once semantics) to stakeholders and downstream teams

- Design and code reviews
  - Participate in design reviews for SQS-based components, challenging inappropriate uses and suggesting better patterns
  - Review code for producers and consumers to ensure correct usage of SQS APIs, error handling, and idempotency

- Operational runbooks and playbooks
  - Contribute to or maintain runbooks describing how to handle common SQS incidents (backlogs, DLQ surges, misconfigurations)
  - Ensure that on-call engineers have clear, up-to-date guidance for interacting with queues during incidents

- Knowledge sharing and mentoring
  - Help more junior engineers understand fundamental SQS concepts, correct mental models, and safe usage patterns
  - Share learnings from incidents and projects to continuously improve team-wide SQS competency","is_non_core_section":true}]}
